"""Stream J browser tests on an invented website, served by Playwright's request routing: no network, no model. They need Chromium (`uv run playwright install chromium`).""" import asyncio import sys import time import unittest from pathlib import Path sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent)) from browser import Tab # noqa: E402 from browsing import BrowsingAgent # noqa: E402 SITE = "https://shop.example.test" LOGIN = """
""" class FakeSite: """A tiny website: a sign-in form, pages behind a session cookie, a page that fails once with 503.""" def __init__(self): self.fail_next = 0 async def handle(self, route): request = route.request path = request.url[len(SITE):] or "/" signed_in = "session=ok" in (await request.all_headers()).get("cookie", "") if path.startswith("/login") and request.method == "POST": return await route.fulfill(status=302, headers={"location": "/orders", "set-cookie": "session=ok; Path=/"}) if path.startswith("/flaky") and self.fail_next: self.fail_next -= 1 return await route.fulfill(status=503, content_type="text/html", body="

Service unavailable

") if not signed_in: return await route.fulfill(status=200, content_type="text/html", body=f"

Sign in

{LOGIN}") pages = { "/orders": '

Orders

Order 2', "/orders/2": '

Order 2

Total 17 units

' 'Total 999 units' 'approved', "/popup": '

Catalogue

Item list

Quick survey

' '
', "/flaky": "

Report

All good

", } body = pages.get(path.split("?")[0], "

Not found

") await route.fulfill(status=200, content_type="text/html", body=body) class BrowserPagesTest(unittest.TestCase): def run_async(self, coroutine_function): async def wrapper(): from playwright.async_api import async_playwright async with async_playwright() as playwright: browser = await playwright.chromium.launch(headless=True) context = await browser.new_context() site = FakeSite() await context.route(f"{SITE}/**", site.handle) page = await context.new_page() await page.goto(f"{SITE}/orders") Tab.homes.clear() tab = Tab("shop", page) try: return await coroutine_function(tab, site, context) finally: await browser.close() return asyncio.run(wrapper()) @staticmethod def agent(tab): return BrowsingAgent(None, {"shop": tab}, {"shop": {"username": "me", "password": "REDACTED"}}, "task", "context", name="t", deadline=time.time() + 60, log=lambda *_: None) def test_hidden_decoys_are_dropped_and_tooltips_resolved(self): async def check(tab, site, context): agent = self.agent(tab) await agent._run_tool("login", {}) return await tab.goto(f"{SITE}/orders/2") view = self.run_async(check) self.assertIn("Total 17 units", view) self.assertNotIn("999", view) self.assertIn("tooltip: approved", view) def test_open_dialog_is_shown_first(self): async def check(tab, site, context): await self.agent(tab)._run_tool("login", {}) return await tab.goto(f"{SITE}/popup") view = self.run_async(check) body = view.split("\n", 2)[2] # after the URL and title lines self.assertTrue(body.startswith("=== OPEN DIALOG"), body[:200]) self.assertLess(body.index("Quick survey"), body.index("Catalogue")) self.assertEqual(view.count("Quick survey"), 1) def test_a_server_error_page_is_reloaded(self): async def check(tab, site, context): await self.agent(tab)._run_tool("login", {}) site.fail_next = 1 return await tab.goto(f"{SITE}/flaky") view = self.run_async(check) self.assertIn("All good", view) def test_expired_session_signs_in_again_and_returns(self): async def check(tab, site, context): agent = self.agent(tab) first = await agent._run_tool("login", {}) self.assertIn("Orders", first) await agent._run_tool("goto", {"url": "/orders/2"}) await context.clear_cookies() # the session expires view = await agent._run_tool("goto", {"url": "/orders/2"}) return agent, view, tab.page.url agent, view, url = self.run_async(check) self.assertEqual(agent.relogins, 1) self.assertIn("session had expired", view) self.assertIn("Total 17 units", view) self.assertTrue(url.endswith("/orders/2"), url) if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()

They need Chromium (`uv run playwright install chromium`).""" import asyncio import sys import time import unittest from pathlib import Path sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent)) from browser import Tab # noqa: E402 from browsing import BrowsingAgent # noqa: E402 SITE = "https://shop.example.test" LOGIN = """
""" class FakeSite: """A tiny website: a sign-in form, pages behind a session cookie, a page that fails once with 503.""" def __init__(self): self.fail_next = 0 async def handle(self, route): request = route.request path = request.url[len(SITE):] or "/" signed_in = "session=ok" in (await request.all_headers()).get("cookie", "") if path.startswith("/login") and request.method == "POST": return await route.fulfill(status=302, headers={"location": "/orders", "set-cookie": "session=ok; Path=/"}) if path.startswith("/flaky") and self.fail_next: self.fail_next -= 1 return await route.fulfill(status=503, content_type="text/html", body="

Service unavailable

") if not signed_in: return await route.fulfill(status=200, content_type="text/html", body=f"

Sign in

{LOGIN}") pages = { "/orders": '

Orders

Order 2', "/orders/2": '

Order 2

Total 17 units

' 'Total 999 units' 'approved', "/popup": '

Catalogue

Item list

Quick survey

' '
', "/flaky": "

Report

All good

", } body = pages.get(path.split("?")[0], "

Not found

") await route.fulfill(status=200, content_type="text/html", body=body) class BrowserPagesTest(unittest.TestCase): def run_async(self, coroutine_function): async def wrapper(): from playwright.async_api import async_playwright async with async_playwright() as playwright: browser = await playwright.chromium.launch(headless=True) context = await browser.new_context() site = FakeSite() await context.route(f"{SITE}/**", site.handle) page = await context.new_page() await page.goto(f"{SITE}/orders") Tab.homes.clear() tab = Tab("shop", page) try: return await coroutine_function(tab, site, context) finally: await browser.close() return asyncio.run(wrapper()) @staticmethod def agent(tab): return BrowsingAgent(None, {"shop": tab}, {"shop": {"username": "me", "password": "REDACTED"}}, "task", "context", name="t", deadline=time.time() + 60, log=lambda *_: None) def test_hidden_decoys_are_dropped_and_tooltips_resolved(self): async def check(tab, site, context): agent = self.agent(tab) await agent._run_tool("login", {}) return await tab.goto(f"{SITE}/orders/2") view = self.run_async(check) self.assertIn("Total 17 units", view) self.assertNotIn("999", view) self.assertIn("tooltip: approved", view) def test_open_dialog_is_shown_first(self): async def check(tab, site, context): await self.agent(tab)._run_tool("login", {}) return await tab.goto(f"{SITE}/popup") view = self.run_async(check) body = view.split("\n", 2)[2] # after the URL and title lines self.assertTrue(body.startswith("=== OPEN DIALOG"), body[:200]) self.assertLess(body.index("Quick survey"), body.index("Catalogue")) self.assertEqual(view.count("Quick survey"), 1) def test_a_server_error_page_is_reloaded(self): async def check(tab, site, context): await self.agent(tab)._run_tool("login", {}) site.fail_next = 1 return await tab.goto(f"{SITE}/flaky") view = self.run_async(check) self.assertIn("All good", view) def test_expired_session_signs_in_again_and_returns(self): async def check(tab, site, context): agent = self.agent(tab) first = await agent._run_tool("login", {}) self.assertIn("Orders", first) await agent._run_tool("goto", {"url": "/orders/2"}) await context.clear_cookies() # the session expires view = await agent._run_tool("goto", {"url": "/orders/2"}) return agent, view, tab.page.url agent, view, url = self.run_async(check) self.assertEqual(agent.relogins, 1) self.assertIn("session had expired", view) self.assertIn("Total 17 units", view) self.assertTrue(url.endswith("/orders/2"), url) if __name__ == "__main__": unittest.main()

content.text:
The hang is fixed in the code, though not yet confirmed live. Survey-4 is running now; it should end within about 10 minutes, and I'll report as soon as it does.

**What happened:**
- **The hang:** the ERP assistant got stuck inside a browser action after its first click. Nothing limited how long an action could take, so the survey waited forever.
- **Why I couldn't trace it:** when I reproduced the step directly, it worked in 3 s. It did show the ERP returning a flaky 503 page at exactly that point, so the hang was probably a page read or reload during navigation.

**The fix:** every browser action now has a 60 s limit, and never past the deadline. Reading each frame of a page has a 10 s limit. The first page view is bounded too. A stuck action now returns "did not finish, use look or goto" to the model instead of freezing everything. A new unit test proves this.

**Also seen live:** the 503 retry from Step 2 did its job. The ERP served a 503 after the consent click, and the page was reloaded and worked.

# Push log · Julien · stream J: sites and reading

Newest entry on top. Format and rules: [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md), section "Push log".

## 2026-10-10 16:00 · Survey harness, own-site guard, sourced notes, wrap-up report

- Changed:
  - `tests/test_browser_survey.py` (new): runs one sub-agent per website with a generic survey task against the
    scouting logins and writes stats (time, actions, finished, notes, notes with source, refused requests). It is
    skipped unless `SURVEY=1`; reports go to the git-ignored `scouting/survey/`.
  - `browser.py`: every `Tab` records the origin it started on (`Tab.homes`).
  - `browsing.py`:
    - `goto` and `download` refuse addresses of another website of the same run; unknown hosts stay allowed.
    - `note` takes a `source` (document, date, sender, revision/status) and is stamped with site, page title and
      URL.
    - `finish` asks for a FOUND / NOT FOUND report.
    - A sub-agent that runs out of steps or time writes that report from its notes in one tool-less call, with Qwen
      reasoning switched off, a token cap and at most 90 s. If that call fails too, a report is built in code from
      the notes and the visited pages.
    - Reminders after 6 actions without a note and 3 steps before the limit.
    - Each model call is bounded by the deadline.
    - New prompt rule: look for newer versions before relying on a record.
  - `tests/test_browser_scope.py` (new): 10 offline tests on invented hosts.
- Why: in the first local run sub-agents opened other sites' pages in their own browser, reports had no sources,
  and three of four sub-agents stopped at the step limit with no usable report. One of those had noted only an
  older, superseded record.
- Checked:
  - Unit tests: the 10 new ones pass. The 3 errors in `tests/test_kit.py` are older (the starter test still expects
    `solve()`).
  - Two four-site surveys with Qwen (40 steps per site). Notes with a source: 15/15 and 23/23. Sub-agents that
    finished: 1/4, then 2/4. Notes on the ERP: 1, then 4.
  - The mail sub-agent now finds the governing approval and labels the older one and the look-alikes as such.
  - A forced cross-site task was refused 3 times and the item was reported under NOT FOUND.
  - The wrap-up report was checked live.
- Learned:
  - Qwen reasons before answering. With a token cap the reasoning can use up the whole cap, and the answer then
    comes back empty. Reasoning can be switched off per call (`enable_thinking: False` via `extra_body`).
  - Qwen calls sometimes take minutes, probably when the team's 32 shared slots are full.
  - The shared scouting mailbox collects signing-code mails from everyone's runs.
- For the others:
  - O: `Tab` and `BrowsingAgent` keep the same constructor and `run()` return type.
  - O: reasoning tokens are a large share of time and cost per call; switching reasoning off where it isn't needed
    is worth testing in the lead.
  - O: `tests/test_kit.py` fails on `main`.
  - I: nothing.
- Next: Step 2: re-login when a session expires, retry error pages, show open dialogs first in the page view.

content.text: what would be the correct choice here?

Open the pull request first, then continue with Step 3 on your branch. Both happen in parallel, so it costs only a few minutes. Why:

1. **Orhun needs it now.** His sandbox test runs and the baseline score run from `main`. Until then they use the old sub-agents, the ones that wandered to other sites, hung and returned reports without sources. Every test run he does before the merge measures problems we've already fixed.
2. **It's what the team rules intend.** `main` is meant to be "what works", and the PR is the hand-over between streams. Steps 0–2 are tested, the interfaces are unchanged, and they ran stably live, so they meet that bar.
3. **You can merge it yourself.** It only touches stream-J files; the merge of `main` is already included. Per the rules you merge your own PR, using "Create a merge commit" so the Entire checkpoints stay.
4. **A smaller merge is less risky.** Waiting until Step 3 is done makes the change bigger and gives the teammates' work more time to diverge.

The remaining risk is small. Re-login and dialogs-first haven't triggered live, but they only kick in when a password form or dialog appears, and the PR description will say so.

**End-to-end run:** about 3.5 minutes in, running normally. The lead model sent all four sub-agents out at 36 s, and they have made 92 actions so far with no errors, hangs or wandering. A full run takes up to about 20 minutes. I'll open the PR once it has gone through cleanly.

- **`collect_pages` tool:** the model picks the "next page" or "load more" control, and the code follows it to the end and joins the pages. Repeated page chrome is shown once. Tested with both a paged list and a JavaScript "load more" button.

It now fetches inside the page, with the old client as a fallback. Tested with a ZIP (CSV plus a file in a subfolder) and a PDF.

content.text:
The wrap-up timed out for tender portal and mail, after 30 s each. They fell back to the code-built report (notes plus visited pages), so nothing was lost, but those reports have no FOUND / NOT FOUND structure.

The cause is in my design: browsing ran right up to the deadline, so the wrap-up started *after* it and got only the 30 s minimum. Qwen was busy with five agents at once and couldn't write a full report in that time. The fix:
- **Reserve 45 s:** browsing stops 45 s before the deadline, so the wrap-up fits *within* the lead's deadline instead of after it. That also respects Orhun's time plan better.
- **Shorter wrap-up:** a cap of 2,000 tokens with short lines, so it finishes faster.

content.text:
The 5/100 run is `run_5c4a1b2fa02c4d4c`, a sandbox test run from 13:24. That was **before** PR #3 was merged at 13:47, so it used the old sub-agents.

**What the scorer saw:** it answered `no_bid` with no positions. It got only the tender reference (5 points). The correct answer is a **bid**: the scorer expects positions 01.01–01.05. A wrong `no_bid` is the most expensive mistake possible because it forfeits nearly everything:

| Lost | Points |
|---|---|
| decision (bid) | 5 |
| all 5 positions (material, quantity, prices, lead time…) | ~65 |
| discount, total, arithmetic consistency | 15 |
| withdrawn-Q&A check, metal-index-window check | 10 |

**Why it happened, as a chain:**
1. **The sub-agents couldn't deliver ERP data** (stream J). The ERP was behind its entry gate, Qwen calls stalled, and steps ran out. That's what PR #3 and Step 3 fix: the ERP sub-agent now passes the gate and reaches materials, though it still runs short of steps before the prices.
2. **The lead mixed up "not found" with "doesn't exist"** (stream O). Rule 3 says *no_bid if a position has no matching active material*. The lead had no ERP data, concluded "no material", and chose no_bid. That's the real logic error: missing evidence isn't evidence of absence. A partial bid would have scored clearly more. Quantities alone come from the tender (15 % of each position), and the decision, discount and reference come from other sites.

**What I can do in stream J (fits Step 4):** make reports clearly separate the two kinds of NOT FOUND:
- **"checked, does not exist":** e.g. "catalogue group searched, all N hits opened, no active exact match"
- **"not checked / not reachable":** e.g. "ERP gate not passed", "price tab not opened"

Then the lead can only justify no_bid with the first kind.

**For Orhun (stream O):** the lead should only choose `no_bid` when a report confirms "checked, does not exist" for a position. Otherwise bid, and omit or partially fill the unclear positions. I'd suggest you pass that on to him; it's his file.

Should I build the NOT FOUND split into Step 4?

`main` had new code, so I merged it into `stream-j` (`b8d7e62`, no conflicts). It's Ivan's (stream I) work: `facts.py` with a `FactsBuilder`, an engine that keeps the answer valid even with damaged facts, a bid explanation for the run log, and **"no_bid names closest candidates"**. None of my files changed.

## What the new code means for Step 4

1. **Sources have a fixed shape now.** `facts.Source` = site, document, date, sender, revision, note. My notes currently take `source` as one free-text string, so Orhun's lead has to pick it apart again. If notes deliver exactly these fields, the report → facts mapping becomes direct.

2. **The engine's no_bid relies on a weak signal.** `resolve.searched()` counts a catalogue group as "searched" if it's listed in `searched_groups` **or if any one candidate of that group is known**. So if the ERP sub-agent opened only 1 of 5 hits, the engine treats the group as searched. If the matching material wasn't among those opened, it chooses **no_bid**, which is the 5-point disaster from the test run, now in deterministic form. Reports must therefore say **how complete** a search was: "group X: N hits, all N opened" versus "2 of 5 opened".

3. **`SpecRevision.current` and `DiscountApproval.reference`** match Step 4's two topics, versions and look-alikes. Reports must deliver exactly those values: which revision is marked current, and the exact reference of every approval or rule mail.

## Plan for Step 4 (only stream-J files)

1. **Structured sources in `note`.** Separate fields `document`, `date`, `sender`, `revision`, `status` (e.g. current / superseded / draft) and `reference` (the exact tender reference the record names), shaped like `facts.Source`. The page stamp stays automatic.
2. **Versions.** For versioned records the report lists all versions found, with date and status. It says which one the site marks as current and on what basis (a marker or the latest date), and which version each value comes from.
3. **Look-alikes.** Every record gets its exact reference, sender and date. Records for a different reference (e.g. a suffix like `-A`), from an unauthorised sender or dated after the scenario date are listed as **look-alike / not applicable**, never under FOUND.
4. **Split NOT FOUND**, also in the wrap-up report:
   - **CHECKED, NOT PRESENT:** with the search coverage, "search X: N hits, all opened, none matches".
   - **NOT CHECKED:** not reached, cut off, or only partly opened, "2 of 5 hits opened".
5. **Live check** against the scout notes, on the mail site (superseded approvals, `-A` look-alikes, future-dated mails) and the supplier portal (revision marked current).

**For the teammates** (please pass on, since it's their files):
- **Ivan:** `searched()` should only count a group as searched if the report confirms the search was *complete*. A single known candidate isn't enough.
- **Orhun:** the lead should only allow `no_bid` with "CHECKED, NOT PRESENT" evidence.

No. Step 4 doesn't benefit from agents, and it would cost noticeably more Claude tokens:

- **The work is small and connected.** Almost everything happens in `browsing.py`: the note schema, the report structure, prompt rules and the wrap-up, plus tests. These parts depend on each other, so they can't be split into independent pieces for agents to work on in parallel.
- **Each agent starts from zero.** It would first have to read `CLAUDE.md`, `streams.md`, `browsing.py` and `facts.py`, which I already know. That's tens of thousands of tokens per agent before it writes a single line.
- **The slow part is the live test, and that's free:** Qwen surveys take minutes, and agents can't speed that up.

Agents are worth it for broad, independent searches or reviews. A use case could come later in Step 5 (checking all my files for anything tied to the public sites), and even there a grep would probably do.

## 2026-10-10 19:10 · Versions, look-alikes, and two kinds of "not found"

- Changed: `browsing.py`:
  - `note` takes structured source fields shaped like `facts.Source`: `document`, `date`, `sender`, `revision`,
    `status` and `reference` (free `source` text stays optional).
  - Reports and the wrap-up now have four parts: FOUND; SUPERSEDED / LOOK-ALIKE; CHECKED, NOT PRESENT (with
    search evidence); NOT CHECKED.
  - Prompt rules:
    - Find all versions and say which one is marked current and on what basis.
    - Check every record's reference character for character, its sender and its date against the scenario date.
    - Report something as absent only after a complete search.
  - Test for the source fields in `tests/test_browser_scope.py`.
- Why: a sandbox test run scored 5 of 100 because the lead answered no_bid after the ERP data never arrived; "not
  found" was read as "does not exist". The bid engine's `resolve.searched()` also counts a catalogue group as
  searched as soon as one candidate is known, so reports must say how complete a search was.
- Checked:
  - 13 scope tests pass.
  - Live survey with Qwen on the mailbox and the supplier portal, compared with what is on the websites:
    - The governing record is under FOUND with all source fields.
    - Look-alike references, drafts and a record dated after the scenario date are under SUPERSEDED /
      LOOK-ALIKE.
    - The current revision is named with its basis, and the older revisions are listed as superseded.
    - Every note has a source.
- Not checked: the mail sub-agent ran out of steps before the archive and the second result page. It listed the
  result page under NOT CHECKED but not the archive folder.
- Learned: a record dated after the scenario date is easy to miss without an explicit date check; with the rule
  the model rejected one.
- For the others:
  - O: use the four parts. Only CHECKED, NOT PRESENT supports a no_bid; NOT CHECKED means unknown.
  - I: `resolve.searched()` would be safer if a group counted as searched only when a report confirms the search
    was complete.
- Next: Step 5 (generalisation check), then Step 6 (fewer steps per report).

# Push log · Julien · stream J: sites and reading

Newest entry on top. Format and rules: [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md), section "Push log".

## 2026-10-10 18:30 · Paged lists, documents, model stalls, wrap-up inside the deadline

- Changed:
  - `browser.py`:
    - New `collect_pages`: follows a "next page" or "load more" control the model chose, and returns the views
      joined.
    - Frames that load late (e.g. after a collapsed section opens) are waited for, at most 3 s.
    - `download` now fetches inside the page (same cookies, proxy and network as the browser), with Playwright's
      own client only as a fallback.
  - `browsing.py`:
    - The `collect_pages` tool.
    - Each model call is capped at 75 s and retried up to 3 times while the deadline allows.
    - Browsing stops 45 s before the deadline, so the wrap-up report fits inside it; the wrap-up is shorter.
    - Prompt rules: use `collect_pages` for lists; refine a search that shows nothing; open a record's tabs or
      registers before reporting a value as missing.
  - Tests: `test_browser_pages.py` covers paging, "load more", a late frame, and ZIP and PDF downloads;
    `test_browser_scope.py` covers a stalled model call.
- Why: in a full local run of `agent.py` the lead submitted with every position omitted. The ERP sub-agent lost
  about five minutes to a single stalled Qwen call and hit the deadline. Two wrap-up reports timed out because they
  started after the deadline. The download fix came out of a test: Playwright's own HTTP client does not go through
  the page's network, so in the sandbox it would probably miss the browser's proxy.
- Checked:
  - 21 stream-J tests pass.
  - ERP-only survey with Qwen: one stall was cut at 75 s and the retry answered in 2.5 s. The sub-agent passed the
    ERP's entry gate (slider, checkbox, receipt number, acknowledgement) and reached materials, stock and
    conditions.
  - Every ERP note has a source.
  - Re-login confirmed live in the full run: after the session expired the mail sub-agent signed in again, cleared
    the consent page and went back to the archive page it was reading.
- Not fixed: the ERP sub-agent still runs out of steps before opening every sub-view. Prices sit in a separate
  register of each condition record. The new prompt rule is not yet checked live.
- Learned:
  - Some websites gate the whole application behind a notice page that needs several controls. A model gets past
    it when it is given the time.
  - Price amounts can be one click deeper than the record that names them.
- For the others: O: a sub-agent now always returns within its deadline. The full run showed the submission
  sub-agent ending after 2 steps for a bid without positions. I: nothing.
- Next: Step 4 (versions and look-alikes in reports), then fewer steps per report.

## 2026-10-10 17:40 · Sessions, errors, dialogs, no more hangs

- Changed:
  - `browsing.py`:
    - After a successful `login`, an action that lands on a sign-in form signs in again by itself and returns to
      the page before the action.
    - Every browser action is bounded (60 s, never past the deadline), and so is the first page view; a stuck
      action reports "did not finish" to the model.
  - `browser.py`:
    - The HTTP status of each page load is recorded; a 5xx page is reloaded up to twice, and the page view says so.
    - Reading each frame is bounded to 10 s.
  - `observe.js`: open dialogs and modals are shown first in the page view, marked as in front of the page, and
    not repeated below.
  - Tests:
    - `tests/test_browser_pages.py` (new): headless Chromium against an invented site served by request routing,
      no network. Covers re-login, the 5xx reload, dialogs first, and hidden decoys and tooltips.
    - `tests/test_browser_scope.py`: a hanging browser action no longer holds the agent.
    - `tests/test_browser_survey.py`: also counts re-logins.
- Why: the brief warns of expiring sessions, flaky error pages and popups. In one survey a sub-agent hung inside a
  single browser action for eight minutes and held up the whole run.
- Checked:
  - 15 unit tests pass.
  - Four-site survey with Qwen: 3/4 sub-agents finished by themselves (best so far), 21/21 notes with a source, no
    hangs. The fourth was stopped by the time limit, and its wrap-up report says plainly what it did not read.
  - The 5xx reload worked live on one website right after the consent page.
- Not checked live:
  - Re-login: no session expired during the 5-minute surveys.
  - Dialogs first: reports do not contain page views, so this is verified only by the offline test.
  - The original hang did not reproduce on demand, so the fix rests on the bound and its unit test.
- Learned:
  - Websites can answer 5xx right after a form step and work on a reload.
  - A Playwright read of a frame that is mid-navigation can wait without limit, so every read needs a bound.
- For the others: O: nothing changes in the interfaces; sub-agents now always return before their deadline plus
  the wrap-up (at most 90 s). I: nothing.
- Next: Step 3, documents and lists (PDF, ZIP, frames, paging, "load more", over-broad searches).

## 2026-10-10 16:00 · Survey harness, own-site guard, sourced notes, wrap-up report

- Changed:
  - `tests/test_browser_survey.py` (new): runs one sub-agent per website with a generic survey task against the
    scouting logins and writes stats (time, actions, finished, notes, notes with source, refused requests). It is
    skipped unless `SURVEY=1`; reports go to the git-ignored `scouting/survey/`.
  - `browser.py`: every `Tab` records the origin it started on (`Tab.homes`).
  - `browsing.py`:
    - `goto` and `download` refuse addresses of another website of the same run; unknown hosts stay allowed.
    - `note` takes a `source` (document, date, sender, revision/status) and is stamped with site, page title and
      URL.
    - `finish` asks for a FOUND / NOT FOUND report.
    - A sub-agent that runs out of steps or time writes that report from its notes in one tool-less call, with Qwen
      reasoning switched off, a token cap and at most 90 s. If that call fails too, a report is built in code from
      the notes and the visited pages.
    - Reminders after 6 actions without a note and 3 steps before the limit.
    - Each model call is bounded by the deadline.
    - New prompt rule: look for newer versions before relying on a record.
  - `tests/test_browser_scope.py` (new): 10 offline tests on invented hosts.
- Why: in the first local run sub-agents opened other sites' pages in their own browser, reports had no sources,
  and three of four sub-agents stopped at the step limit with no usable report. One of those had noted only an
  older, superseded record.
- Checked:
  - Unit tests: the 10 new ones pass. The 3 errors in `tests/test_kit.py` are older (the starter test still expects
    `solve()`).
  - Two four-site surveys with Qwen (40 steps per site). Notes with a source: 15/15 and 23/23. Sub-agents that
    finished: 1/4, then 2/4. Notes on the ERP: 1, then 4.
  - The mail sub-agent now finds the governing approval and labels the older one and the look-alikes as such.
  - A forced cross-site task was refused 3 times and the item was reported under NOT FOUND.
  - The wrap-up report was checked live.
- Learned:
  - Qwen reasons before answering. With a token cap the reasoning can use up the whole cap, and the answer then
    comes back empty. Reasoning can be switched off per call (`enable_thinking: False` via `extra_body`).
  - Qwen calls sometimes take minutes, probably when the team's 32 shared slots are full.
  - The shared scouting mailbox collects signing-code mails from everyone's runs.
- For the others:
  - O: `Tab` and `BrowsingAgent` keep the same constructor and `run()` return type.
  - O: reasoning tokens are a large share of time and cost per call; switching reasoning off where it isn't needed
    is worth testing in the lead.
  - O: `tests/test_kit.py` fails on `main`.
  - I: nothing.
- Next: Step 2: re-login when a session expires, retry error pages, show open dialogs first in the page view.

        """A popup that closes itself (e.g. a search help after a selection): go back to the page below it."""
        if page is not self.page:

            self.previous.pop()
        if self.previous:

            self.events.append("The active page had closed; back on the previous page")

        self._attach_page_only(self.page)

## 2026-10-10 20:10 · Generalisation and fewer steps: ARIA grids, shadow DOM, read_pages, popups

- Changed:
  - `observe.js` (step 5, generalisation): tables built from elements with ARIA roles (`grid`, `row`, `cell`)
    render as rows; content inside open shadow roots (web components) is read; more control roles are numbered
    (`combobox`, `treeitem`, `textbox`, `slider` and others).
  - `browser.py`:
    - New `read_pages`: up to 6 pages the model chose, rendered in parallel background tabs and returned in one
      step (step 6).
    - Popups: only popups this tab opened are followed. When a popup closes itself, the tab returns to the page
      that opened it. If the active page closed for any other reason, it falls back to an earlier page or reopens
      the site.
  - `browsing.py`: the `read_pages` tool (addresses of other websites are refused one by one); the page view
    before the newest is cut to 4000 characters.
  - Tests: ARIA grid, shadow DOM and combobox; `read_pages`; a popup that closes itself; view shortening.
- Why:
  - Step 5: the private dataset uses different software. A string search found nothing tied to the public sites
    in stream J's files, so the work went into page structures the public sites do not use.
  - Step 6: sub-agents spent most turns opening pages whose links they could already see.
  - In one survey the ERP sub-agent's tab stayed on a popup that had closed itself, and every later action failed.
- Checked:
  - 25 stream-J tests pass. The popup test fails on the previous `browser.py` with the same error the survey
    showed, and passes now.
  - Survey 5 (with `read_pages`): all four sub-agents finished by themselves for the first time; the mail sub-agent
    noted 11 facts instead of 4.
  - Survey 6: no closed-page errors, and the ERP report reaches the price scales.
- Not as hoped:
  - Survey 6 finished only 1/4 by itself. Five model calls stalled (75 s each), so the two surveys are not
    comparable on finishing.
  - Input tokens per call fell only about 3 % (12.0k to 11.7k); the brief and the newest view dominate.
  - `read_pages` raised the total input tokens of a survey by about 30 %, because more page content is read.
- Learned:
  - Survey results vary strongly with Qwen load; compare several runs before drawing conclusions on speed.
  - Websites open helper popups that close themselves after a choice.
- For the others: O: sub-agents receive the lead's full brief as context. Giving them only the task part would
  shrink every call, though the brief is a stable, cached prefix. I: nothing.
- Next: steps 0–6 are done. Next is a full local run of `agent.py` and the score of a sandbox test run (through O).

source.data:
Stream I (Ivan) reviewed the package and found issues in stream J's files. Fix them on stream-j (git switch
stream-j, git pull, git merge origin/main first). Edit only stream J's files (browser.py, observe.js, browsing.py,
browsers.py, tests/test_browser*). Details are also in docs/log/ivan.md, latest entry.

1. observe.js, the `clean` function (around line 11): the regex contains raw invisible characters (zero-width
   spaces and the left-to-right/right-to-left marks U+200E/U+200F). Raw direction marks in source are what linters
   and code reviewers flag as obfuscated code, and Atira's AI reviewer reads every package. Write the character
   class with escapes: /[\u200b-\u200f\u2060\ufeff\u00ad]/g. Then check the whole package for raw invisible
   characters (a short Python loop over the files looking for code points 0x200B-0x200F, 0x2060, 0xFEFF, 0xAD,
   0x202A-0x202E, 0x2066-0x2069) and escape any you find in your files.
2. browser.py line 12: OBSERVE_JS is read with read_text() without encoding; on Windows that decodes as cp1252
   and fails. Use read_text(encoding="utf-8").
3. observe.js, `describe` for INPUT: a password input prints its value (value="..."), so a filled login password
   or a TAN typed into a password-type field goes into the model's prompt and the run log. For type=password,
   show only whether it is filled (e.g. value=<filled>/<empty>).
4. browser.py `_HtmlText.handle_endtag`: a stray </script> or </style> makes `skip` negative, and then all later
   text is dropped (the check is `if not self.skip`). Clamp it: self.skip = max(0, self.skip - 1).
5. browser.py `fetch_file`: for an HTML URL the page is fetched once with fetch() and then loaded again in a
   scratch tab, so a GET with side effects (e.g. a logout or cancel link) runs twice. Render the HTML already
   fetched (e.g. set it as the scratch page's content with the URL as base) instead of loading the URL a second
   time, or at least skip the first fetch for HTML.
6. browsing.py `run`: when the model sends several tool calls in one turn and `finish` comes before a `note`, the
   function returns at `finish` and the later note is lost. Run all non-finish calls of the turn first, then
   handle finish.
7. browsing.py `_shows_sign_in`: any visible password field counts as an expired session, so a password-type TAN
   or code field on a normal page triggers an automatic re-login and a jump back to the previous URL. Only treat
   it as a sign-in page if the form also has a user-name field, or the URL looks like a sign-in page
   (_looks_like_sign_in_url), or the page was not a password page before the action.

Add a test for 3, 4 and 6 in tests/test_browser*.py with invented pages only. Run
`uv run python -m unittest discover -s tests` in agent/ (the engine tests must stay green), add a push log entry
to docs/log/julien.md, commit with "J: ..." and push to stream-j.

## 2026-10-10 20:45 · Review fixes from stream I

- Changed: all seven findings from Ivan's review (`docs/log/ivan.md`, 16:29):
  1. `observe.js`: the cleaning pattern uses escapes instead of raw invisible characters. A scan of every package
     file for zero-width, direction-mark and soft-hyphen code points now finds none.
  2. `browser.py` reads `observe.js` as UTF-8 explicitly.
  3. `observe.js`: password fields show only `value=<filled>` or `value=<empty>`, never their value.
  4. `browser.py`: a stray closing `script`/`style` tag no longer hides the rest of a document's text.
  5. `browser.py`: an HTML download renders the bytes it already fetched instead of requesting the address a
     second time.
  6. `browsing.py`: calls sent in one turn run before `finish`, so a note sent with `finish` is kept.
  7. `browsing.py`: an expired session is detected only when a sign-in form appears (password plus user-name field,
     or a sign-in address) on a page that had no password field before. A code field alone no longer triggers a
     re-login.
  - Tests for 3–7 in `tests/test_browser_*`, invented pages only.
- Why: the review found these in stream J's files. Raw direction marks read as obfuscation to a reviewer, a
  password in the page view reaches the prompt and the logs, and the others lose text or notes, or repeat requests.
- Checked:
  - 161 unit tests run, including stream I's engine tests. The only failures are the 3 known ones in
    `tests/test_kit.py`.
  - The five new tests fail on the previous code and pass now.
  - Short live ERP survey: finished by itself in 100 s, no false re-login, every note with a source.
- For the others: I: thanks for the review. O: nothing changes in the interfaces.
- Next: the score breakdown of a sandbox test run with all stream-J changes.

content.text:
Ivan's review was correct: all 7 findings were real bugs in my stream's code. All 7 are now fixed, tested and merged into `main` (PR #7, merge commit `b84a352`). Nothing had been implemented yet when I started, so I did the fixes myself.

| # | Problem | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Invisible characters written raw into `observe.js`, which a reviewer could flag as hidden code | Written as escapes. A scan of the whole package now finds no invisible characters |
| 2 | `observe.js` read without an encoding, which fails on Windows | Read as UTF-8 |
| 3 | **A filled password was shown in the page view**, so it went into Qwen's prompt and the log | Only `<filled>` / `<empty>` is shown |
| 4 | A stray `</script>` tag swallowed the rest of a document's text | The counter can't go below zero |
| 5 | HTML downloads requested the page twice, so a link with side effects (e.g. logout) ran twice | The already-fetched page is reused |
| 6 | A note sent in the same turn as `finish` was lost | All other actions in the turn run before `finish` |
| 7 | A signing-code field (password type) was mistaken for an expired session and triggered a re-login | Only a real sign-in form counts, on a page that had no password field before |

**Checks:**
- **New tests:** Ivan asked for tests for 3, 4 and 6; I also added them for 5 and 7. All **5 new tests fail on the old code and pass on the new**, so they test the actual fixes.
- **Full suite:** 161 tests run. Ivan's engine tests are all green, and the only failures are the 3 known errors in Orhun's `test_kit.py`.
- **Live ERP smoke test:** finished on its own, with no false re-login and every note sourced.

I followed Ivan's instructions: `main` merged into `stream-j` first, only stream-J files changed, push-log entry written, and a `J:` commit.

content.text: so is my stream finished?

Its work list is done. Its goal, by the team's own definition, isn't fully reached yet.

**What's done:** all 8 items for stream J in `docs/streams.md` (my Steps 0–6) are implemented, tested and merged into `main`, including Ivan's review fixes.

**What's not yet reached:** `docs/streams.md` defines stream J as done when *"a report contains every value the task asked for, as shown on the site, each with its source (page or document, date, sender, revision), and says plainly what it could not find."*

| Part of the criterion | Status |
|---|---|
| Every value with its source | ✅ 100 % of notes in every survey |
| Says plainly what it could not find | ✅ split into "checked, not present" and "not checked" |
| **Every value the task asked for** | ❌ **not yet reliable** |

The surveys show gaps in completeness:
- **ERP:** often runs out of steps or time before reaching every price scale, especially when Qwen stalls.
- **Mail:** didn't reach the archive in one run.
- **No sandbox test run yet** with all stream-J changes, so there's no real score breakdown showing how many points reading still costs.

So I'd call the stream **feature-complete but not finished**. The remaining work is exactly the end-to-end validation I proposed: a full agent run plus a sandbox test-run score (through Orhun), then closing the completeness gaps that cost points, with the ERP prices first since positions are worth 75 points.

Should I start on that as Step 7?

content.text: so is step 7 part of orhuns stream or mine?

Mostly yours, with one part that runs through Orhun:

| Part | Whose | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Making reports **complete**: ERP prices within the budget, the mail archive, fewer missing values | **Yours (J)** | That's your stream's "done" criterion, and the code is in your files |
| Local full runs of the agent (`agent.py` with scouting logins) | **Anyone** | Free and unlimited; you can run them yourself |
| **Starting sandbox test runs** | **Orhun (O)** | Team rule: test runs go through stream O (limit of 2 at a time) |
| Reading the score breakdown and fixing the points **reading** loses | **Yours (J)** | Wrong or missing values from the sites are stream J bugs |
| Points lost through the **lead**: which tasks it gives the sub-agents (e.g. passing on the Kataloggruppen), its time split (65 % collecting), `no_bid` decisions, submission | **Orhun (O)** | `agent.py` and the submission are his files |
| Points lost through **calculation** | **Ivan (I)** | Engine and `facts.py` |

So Step 7 is your stream's work. You only need Orhun for the sandbox runs. In practice: I improve report completeness and check it with local surveys and full runs; when there's a version worth scoring, you ask Orhun for a test run; then we go through the breakdown together and split each lost point into J, O or I.

Should I start Step 7 like that?

entries.name: mcp__atira__run_logs
entries.description: A run's log lines, in time order, each with its time on the run's clock and its stream. Streams: stdout and stderr (your agent system), setup (the platform: install, the free models' warm-up), input (what the browsers received; run_inputs reads them better, so they're left out unless you ask). Narrow with from/to (e.g. from 02:10 to 02:40), grep, browser; tail for the last lines; page with after. About 30 tokens a line.

run_id.description: A run id (run_...) from list_runs, a test run id (reh_...), or a submission id (sub_...: its latest run)

from.description: The earliest time, on the run's clock, as the run page and run_logs show it: mm:ss or h:mm:ss (seconds may have a fraction), 3m20s, or seconds; a minus is before the start. An ISO 8601 time also works.

to.description: The latest time, on the run's clock, as the run page and run_logs show it: mm:ss or h:mm:ss (seconds may have a fraction), 3m20s, or seconds; a minus is before the start. An ISO 8601 time also works.

stream.description: Only these streams, comma-separated: stdout, stderr, setup, input; "all" is every one. Default: stdout, stderr and setup.

grep.description: Only lines containing this text, case-insensitive; a|b matches either

browser.description: Only the platform's lines about this browser (its inputs, a browser it stopped)

tail.description: Only the last n matching lines

after.description: Continue after a previous page: its `next` value

content.text:
The run failed for three reasons. Two are in Orhun's stream; the third is the stream-J bug already fixed in PR #5.

**Timing:** the run started at **14:26 UTC**. My popup fix (PR #5) was merged at 14:32 UTC and the review fixes at 14:42, so **this run did not include them yet**.

**What went wrong, in order:**

1. **ERP crash at 07:33 (stream J, already fixed).** The ERP sub-agent noted: *"Browser session on ERP crashed after clicking the first search result (Target page/context closed)"*. That's exactly the self-closing popup bug: the F4 search help closes itself after a selection, and the tab stayed attached to the closed window. PR #5 fixes it, and the test reproduces this exact error on the old code. As a result, the lead never got status, stock or prices from the ERP.
   - The `getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN` came from the `download` fallback through Playwright's own HTTP client, which can't resolve addresses in the sandbox. It only kicked in because the page was already dead, but it confirms that fallback is useless there. I'd swap it for a fallback through a fresh browser tab, a small stream-J fix.

2. **About 4 minutes of standstill (09:09–13:10, Orhun).** After the reports came in, the **lead's** own Qwen call hung until it timed out at 13:10 (`APITimeoutError`). My 75 s stall cap only applies to sub-agents; the lead's `llm.py` waits much longer.

3. **Submission too late (Orhun).** The lead only started submitting at 1030 s of about 1215 s. The submission sub-agent needed 91 s for a single step, and the run ended before it got past the tender page. With no answer at all, the run scores 0 and isn't eligible.

**What helps:**
- **Orhun:** cap the lead's model calls and retry them (like my 75 s logic), and start the submission earlier or reserve a fixed time block for it. Point 2 alone would have given the submission 4 minutes more.
- **Me (stream J):** the browser-based `download` fallback, about 15 minutes of work.
- **Then a new test run** with the current `main`, which contains the popup fix. Only that shows whether the ERP gets through in the sandbox.

Should I build the `download` fallback now?

read a website. Put what the report states into the facts and call `add_facts` once. Take the tender reference,
the scenario date, the sales director's address and our own mailbox domain from the brief.

- Record every record the report states that the facts have a place for, exactly as stated, each with its source.
- Also record what the report lists as superseded, withdrawn, a look-alike or dated later, with its own source:
  the engine picks the record that counts.
- A catalogue group belongs in `searched_groups` only when the report says the ERP was searched by that group and
  every result was read, also when nothing was found. Leave it out when the report says it was not checked or not
  finished.
- Do not record guesses, and nothing the report says was not checked.
- If the report states nothing that fits, call `add_facts` with an empty object.

content.text:
## Page contract — read before your first publish

These are the Artifact tool's own rules for the file you publish; the design guidance below builds on them.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Skeleton**: The file is wrapped in a `<!doctype html>…<head>…</head><body>` skeleton at publish time, so write the page content directly — no `<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` tags of your own. Its head carries only a charset and viewport meta (with `viewport-fit=cover`) plus a small reset — light `color-scheme`, `:root` padded top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets, zero body margin with a 14px system font, `img{max-width:100%}`, and `[hidden]{display:none!important}` (toggle visibility with `el.hidden`, not `style.display`) — so put your own `<title>` and `<style>` at the top of the file. Keep the `:root` padding: a bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding, and a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, not `0`.

**Title**: Put a `<title>` at the top of the HTML; only the first 8KB of the file is scanned for it. It is the artifact's name in the browser tab and the gallery, so write a name, not a summary: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific enough to pick this page out among many, the way an app or a document is named. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Never use a generic category label alone, and never append an explainer after a dash or colon. If you shorten a title that pairs the name with a generic word, keep the name, not the generic word. A multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished; do not shorten it further. The explanation goes in the one-sentence `description` parameter, which becomes the gallery card's subtitle. The `title` parameter fills in only when an HTML file has no `<title>` tag (Markdown pages keep their filename). Keep the title stable across redeploys.

**External resources — CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external scripts load ONLY from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, https://unpkg.com, https://cdn.tailwindcss.com (Tailwind's play-CDN script) and https://code.jquery.com; external stylesheets ONLY from https://fonts.googleapis.com, with the font files they pull from https://fonts.gstatic.com (give every face a real fallback stack). Everything else is blocked, with no visible error: every other host (esm.sh included) and, even on those CDNs, anything but a script — stylesheets, images, media, fetch/XHR/WebSocket, a library's runtime fetches. So inline all other CSS and JS and embed assets as data: URIs. **How to load a library**: `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/<lib>/<exact version>/<file>">` — pick the UMD build, which defines a global (e.g. react/18.3.1/umd/react.production.min.js, then react-dom) — placed BEFORE any inline `<script>` that uses it. Pin every library URL to an exact version (`react@18.3.1` on jsDelivr or unpkg, `react/18.3.1/…` on cdnjs, `cdn.tailwindcss.com/3.4.17`), never a bare name, a range or a tag (`react`, `react@18`, `@latest`). Choose a version at least two weeks old. Any version you knew before this conversation is old enough; if you look versions up, skip any published in the last two weeks. The viewer's sandbox also blocks any download the page starts itself — `<a download>` links (data:/blob: hrefs included) and script-driven saves are inert for viewers — so never offer a file through a plain link. Links to other websites (`https://…`) open in a new tab, but email, phone and app links (`mailto:`, `tel:`, `sms:`, other custom schemes) are unreliable inside an artifact: for many viewers (for example anyone outside the user's organization, or anyone viewing through a public link) following one, by link or by script, often does not work, and the page cannot tell whether it did. So show the address or number itself as selectable text (a copy button helps), treat such a link as a convenience that may do nothing, and never tell the viewer a message was sent or a call placed because the viewer tapped one. Artifacts render mermaid diagrams natively — markdown via ```mermaid fences, HTML via `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks — no library needed, don't load one. The viewer never shows `alert()`, `confirm()` or `prompt()` dialogs — `confirm()` returns false and `prompt()` returns null immediately — so build any confirmation step into the page itself.

**What the viewer's frame allows**: The page runs in a locked-down frame; what it refuses below, it refuses for every viewer (anonymous, signed-in, embedded, desktop and mobile apps), so build around these limits instead of detecting them. The page cannot open the print dialog — `window.print()` does nothing — so never offer a Print or "Save as PDF" button. Forms work as page UI (inputs, validation, submit events), but a real submission has nowhere to go: handle `submit` in script with `preventDefault()` and never point `action` at another site or a mailto: address. Copy buttons work when `navigator.clipboard.writeText` is called inside the click handler — catch its rejection (older desktop apps and some app views refuse it) and fall back to selecting the text; reading the clipboard never works, though the viewer's own Paste (the `paste` event) does. Camera, microphone, screen capture, location, motion, Web Share and similar device APIs are refused without a prompt — build on one only when this user has a runtime capability for that device (the `artifact-capabilities` skill lists them) and the page declares it; otherwise take photos, audio and data as uploaded files instead (file inputs, drag-and-drop of files and `FileReader` work in browsers). A screen wake lock may be granted while the page is visible: request it and tolerate rejection. Fullscreen and pointer lock work from a click in desktop browsers; treat both as optional (handle the rejection) since phones and some app views lack them. Sound plays only after the viewer interacts (muted autoplay is fine), so start audio from a button. Other sites cannot be embedded — no YouTube, map or form iframes, and no `<object>`/`<embed>`; link out instead: links open outside the artifact, normally in a new tab, while `window.open` works only for some signed-in viewers in the artifact's own organization and returns null for everyone else, so use real `<a href>` links. Web Workers work from your own files or `blob:` URLs; service workers and WebRTC do not. `fetch()` of files published alongside the page works with relative URLs; images from your own files, `data:` or `blob:` URLs draw to canvas and export cleanly. Only a plain `#anchor` (letters, digits, `.` `_` `~` `-`) from the artifact's link reaches `location.hash` — never `#key=value` state and never the query string — so deep-link to a tab or section with a bare token and keep all other state in the page.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Responsive**: The page must also work at phone width (about 400px), and the page body must never scroll horizontally. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, and give that element its vertical padding with `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Use relative units. Let flex and grid rows wrap or stack to one column when narrow, and give any flex or grid child that holds running text, code or a table `min-width: 0`, so long content wraps or scrolls inside it instead of pushing the page wider. Put `max-width: 100%` on images and on any `aspect-ratio` box, and give nothing a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only tables, diagrams and code blocks may be wider, each inside its own `overflow-x: auto` container.

**Theme-aware**: The page renders in the viewer's theme, which has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets nothing, so for most viewers only `prefers-color-scheme` tells light from dark. Define every color as a token, in this shape (token names and count are the design's own):
```css
:root { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: … }  /* every token, light values */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark } }
:root[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark }  /* same dark values, so the toggle wins both ways */
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--fg) }
```
Every token gets its first definition on bare `:root`; the two dark blocks only redefine tokens, and their `color-scheme: dark` makes form controls and scrollbars follow. No color has its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and no component rule uses a literal color that reads in one theme only. `body` keeps that explicit token background: the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body shows the host's theme instead. A dark-first design mirrors the whole shape, selectors included: dark values and `color-scheme: dark` on bare `:root` (the skeleton pins `light` there), light values and `color-scheme: light` under `(prefers-color-scheme: light)` guarded `:root:not([data-theme="dark"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="light"]`. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may drop the two dark blocks but still sets the background and every color explicitly, plus `color-scheme: dark` on `:root` if that look is dark.

**Icon** (on every first publish): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) for the artifact's browser-tab icon — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name, and never an emoji or markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">`, pinned to an exact version at least two weeks old and placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. A bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside that padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets this padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.
